title: API DTO typing end to end
subtitle: Entity, boundaries, Omit leak, FE sync

cards.front: What discipline does end-to-end API DTO typing encode?
cards.meaning: One entity (or domain model) as the persistence source of truth; request DTOs validated at the HTTP boundary; response DTOs that actually omit secrets at runtime, not only in types; awareness of FE/BE sync (shared package / OpenAPI codegen); and why “typed response ⇒ safe” is a trap without validation or mapping.

cards.front: What units does this API DTO discipline sit on?
cards.meaning: Nest DTO patterns, type erasure, utility types / Omit, and unknown vs any.

cards.front: Entity vs create DTO vs response DTO — who owns what?
cards.meaning: Entity owns DB / domain and often holds secrets like passwordHash. Create/update DTOs are inbound HTTP shapes: passwords in plain for input only, never hashes outbound. Response DTOs are outbound HTTP projections with no secrets.

cards.front: What is the canonical field list, and what are DTOs?
cards.meaning: The entity is the canonical field list. Request and response types are projections for directions of travel — inbound vs outbound — not a second copy of the whole domain object.

cards.front: What can “derive” request/response types mean?
cards.meaning: Hand-written response/request classes aligned with the entity; Pick / Omit types for compile-time helpers (not sufficient alone for JSON); or codegen from OpenAPI/GraphQL so FE and BE share a schema.

cards.front: Do @Body() types parse or validate JSON?
cards.meaning: No. Untrusted JSON enters as a plain object. Types on @Body() erase — they do not parse or validate.

cards.front: Where should you validate, and why once?
cards.meaning: Validate/parse once at the HTTP boundary. Inner service code trusts the DTO type because the edge already enforced it. Nest: class-validator plus ValidationPipe (transform, whitelist) on DTO classes. Elsewhere: zod / yup / Valibot schemas — parse → typed value or error.

cards.front: What is z.infer<typeof CreateUser> for?
cards.meaning: The schema is the runtime source of truth; the inferred type stays in sync with parse rules. Alternative to hand-duplicated interfaces for non-Nest stacks.
cards.example: type CreateUser = z.infer<typeof CreateUser>; const dto = CreateUser.parse(req.body);

cards.front: What does CreateUser.parse(req.body) do?
cards.meaning: It throws or returns validated data — parse at the edge, then inner code uses the typed value.

cards.front: Response typed Omit<User,'passwordHash'> but hash still in JSON — how?
cards.meaning: Types erase. Omit only changes what the compiler thinks. If the real object still has passwordHash, JSON.stringify includes it because serializers walk runtime keys. Fix: build an explicit new object/DTO with only public fields (do not cast the entity). In Nest, add @Exclude() plus ClassSerializerInterceptor as a runtime second layer.

cards.front: Why does returning user from toPublic still leak the hash?
cards.meaning: The function can compile because of excess-property / return-compatibility pitfalls, but the object still has the property. Omit changed the type, not the value.
cards.example: function toPublic(user: User): Omit<User, 'passwordHash'> { return user; } // JSON may still include passwordHash

cards.front: How do you prevent the Omit leak structurally?
cards.meaning: Explicitly map to a new object / UserResponseDto (preferred curriculum discipline); in Nest, @Exclude() on sensitive entity fields plus ClassSerializerInterceptor; never use return user as UserResponseDto as your only defense.

cards.front: What should UsersService.create return?
cards.meaning: Hash the password, save the User entity, then return a plain object with only public fields (id, name, email, createdAt). The entity never leaves the service layer directly as the HTTP payload so the runtime object genuinely lacks secrets.
cards.example: return { id: user.id, name: user.name, email: user.email, createdAt: user.createdAt };

cards.front: May the entity leave the service layer as the HTTP payload?
cards.meaning: No. Always map to a response DTO so the runtime object genuinely lacks secrets. Returning entities from controllers “because the return type omits secrets” is the leak.

cards.front: What is the end-to-end DTO flow both directions?
cards.meaning: Client JSON → validate CreateUserDto (pipe / zod) → service hashes password and saves User → map to UserResponseDto (no passwordHash) → optional ClassSerializerInterceptor → JSON response. On the client: fetch should parse with zod/unknown narrow into UI types (shared package or local mirrors).

cards.front: Are both inbound and outbound API edges boundaries?
cards.meaning: Yes. Inbound validation and outbound stripping/mapping on the server; the frontend should not blindly trust network JSON either.

cards.front: How does a shared types package keep FE/BE in sync?
cards.meaning: A monorepo packages/api-types (or similar) imported by Nest and React so both sides use the same TypeScript shapes instead of copy-paste interfaces.

cards.front: How does OpenAPI/Swagger codegen keep FE/BE in sync?
cards.meaning: The backend schema generates a TypeScript client plus types, so the client tracks the published HTTP contract instead of a hand-copied User interface.

cards.front: How does GraphQL codegen keep FE/BE in sync?
cards.meaning: The GraphQL schema generates typed operations and hooks, so operations stay aligned with the schema rather than duplicated models.

cards.front: What is the risk of duplicating User types by hand?
cards.meaning: They drift. Fine only for tiny apps. Prefer schema-first or shared DTOs over copy-paste interface User in two repos with no process.

cards.front: Why does FE/BE type drift hurt in practice?
cards.meaning: The frontend might expect createdAt: string ISO while the backend sends Date serialization quirks, or a field is renamed on one side only. That is the interview-level reason to prefer shared DTOs or codegen.

cards.front: Do shared TypeScript types validate network JSON?
cards.meaning: No. Shared types still do not validate runtime JSON — types erase on both sides. Pair them with zod on the client or a generated client that decodes.

cards.front: Why is (await res.json()) as UserResponseDto unsafe?
cards.meaning: The assertion lies — there is no check that JSON matches. A backend bug or proxy can add fields; XSS-ish assumptions and logic bugs follow. Types erase on both sides. Safer: unknown → schema parse (UserResponseSchema.parse) → typed value, the same boundary idea as Nest pipes.
cards.example: const data = (await res.json()) as UserResponseDto; setUser(data); // trap

cards.front: What is the safer frontend pattern for API JSON?
cards.meaning: Treat the payload as unknown, then schema-parse (e.g. UserResponseSchema.parse) to a typed value. Same boundary idea as Nest pipes.

cards.front: What are Nest’s inbound vs outbound DTO layers?
cards.meaning: Inbound: class-validator DTO classes plus ValidationPipe. Outbound: explicit response mapping and/or @Exclude plus ClassSerializerInterceptor. Compile-time Omit is not a security control.

cards.front: What happens if you forget ValidationPipe whitelist?
cards.meaning: Extra body keys can reach persistence if not stripped. whitelist removes properties without decorator metadata — part of boundary hardening.

cards.front: Why not one type for entity + create + update + response?
cards.meaning: Anti-pattern: secrets and optional PATCH fields get conflated. Derive projections from a canonical entity or schema instead.

cards.front: Is validating only in the UI or only in TypeScript types enough?
cards.meaning: No. The HTTP boundary must parse/validate untrusted JSON. UI checks and TS annotations do not replace a pipe or schema parse on the server (and the client should parse responses too).

cards.front: Is as UserResponseDto or as Omit<…> a security control?
cards.meaning: No. Casts and Omit do not strip runtime fields. Mapping to a new object or serializer exclusion does.

cards.front: How does erasure explain the Omit leak?
cards.meaning: Erasure means Omit and casts do not strip JSON fields. The compiler’s view of the object is not what JSON.stringify walks.

cards.front: What Nest tools are the inbound boundary?
cards.meaning: DTO classes plus ValidationPipe (class-validator / class-transformer) — the request-validation half of the discipline.

cards.front: What tools are the outbound boundary?
cards.meaning: An explicit map to a response DTO, and/or @Exclude plus ClassSerializerInterceptor, so secrets never ride the serialized object.

cards.front: How does unknown + zod on the frontend fit this unit?
cards.meaning: It is the same boundary idea as Nest pipes, applied to responses: do not trust res.json(), parse untrusted data into a typed value.

cards.front: What does a shared package or OpenAPI buy you?
cards.meaning: It reduces type drift across frontend and backend. It still does not validate runtime JSON by itself — pair with parse/codegen decoders.
